steps.title: A narrow valley
steps.body: The northern Rhône runs about 60 km along the Rhône river, from Vienne, south of Lyon, to Valence. Vineyards cling to steep slopes on both banks, mostly granite and schist, often on terraces held by dry-stone walls, called chaillées. It's small: about 5% of all Rhône wine.

steps.title: Continental and steep
steps.body: The climate is continental, cooler than the south, with the Mistral wind blowing down the valley. Steep, south and south-east facing slopes catch the sun and drain cold air, letting Syrah ripen this far north. Terraces stop soil erosion. Work is by hand, sometimes with winches, making the wines costly.

steps.prompt: Why do northern Rhône vineyards use terraces?
options: To hold soil on steep slopes
steps.explanation: Terraces prevent erosion and make work possible.

steps.title: Ancient vineyards
steps.body: Vines have grown here since Roman times; Vienne was an important Roman city, and its wine was praised by Pliny. Hermitage takes its name from a 13th century knight, Gaspard de Stérimberg, who, legend says, lived there as a hermit after the Crusades.
steps.highlight: Roman vines; the hermit of Hermitage

steps.prompt: The northern Rhône makes most of the Rhône's wine.
steps.explanation: Not true. It makes about 5%; the south makes over 90%.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The northern Rhône runs 60 km on steep granite slopes
Steep, sunny slopes ripen Syrah in a continental climate
It's small, about 5% of Rhône wine
